## Roles

ForgeCycle has four roles. Each policy names an ordered candidate
list for each role, and the role flags replace one list for one invocation.

| Role | Runs | Writes | Policy list and flag |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Decomposer | `roadmap decompose`, `roadmap questions` | decomposition JSON, decisions | `decomposer`, `--decomposer` |
| Planner | the `planning` phase | `NNN-planner-plan.md` (`kind: planner_plan`, `role: Planner`) | `planner`, `--planner` |
| Builder | the `building` phase | one commit and `NNN-builder-result.md` (`kind: builder_result`, `role: Builder`) | `builder`, `--builder` |
| Reviewer | the `reviewing` phase | `NNN-reviewer-review.md` (`kind: reviewer_review`, `role: Reviewer`) | `reviewer`, `--reviewer` |

Only Builder changes the repository. Decomposer, Planner, and Reviewer run
read-only; ForgeCycle checks Git state around their turns, and a Planner or
Reviewer turn that changes it stops with `read_only_mutation`.

## Artifact transport

Every model call starts without a resumed vendor conversation. ForgeCycle creates
a turn manifest naming the immutable task snapshot, applicable handoffs, human
feedback, governing files, base revision, worktree, and output contract. The CLI
adapter returns the agent's final message; ForgeCycle validates it and atomically
writes the numbered handoff. The final message must be the handoff itself: it
begins with the `---` front matter delimiter as its very first characters, with
no preamble or explanation around it. Validation failures name the exact field,
the offending value, and the allowed set, so the repair prompt can point the
model at the precise defect.

Every candidate response, initial or repair, passes through one pipeline before
it may be stored (`protocol.PrepareHandoff`):

1. **Canonicalize**. Only named, deterministic rules apply:
   `strip_preamble` (prose before the first `---` line that is followed by a
   `schema_version:` or `kind:` key), `split_glued_delimiter`
   (`---schema_version: 1`), `trim_marker_whitespace`,
   `drop_leading_blank_lines`, `close_frontmatter` (insert the missing
   closing `---` where the block ended at a blank line), and
   `fullwidth_key_colon` (only when the YAML does not otherwise parse). Prose
   with no recognizable handoff opening still fails with the preamble error.
   The body after the closing delimiter is never modified.
2. **Fill orchestrator-owned facts**. `schema_version`, `run_id`,
   `turn`, `base_revision`, `head_revision`, and each required test's
   `command` are inserted when missing. A revision prefix of at least 7
   characters is expanded to the full SHA. A required test command that is
   equivalent to the required one is rewritten to the exact required string.
   A wrong value that is present is never overwritten: a wrong `run_id` or
   `turn` is a binding error, and a wrong revision is a repairable error that
   names the actual value.
3. **Validate** against the turn. Shape, enums and sections are
   checked, along with the currently required tests and configured command
   lint rules.

The stored artifact is the canonical, filled document, with exactly two `---`
lines before the body. When a normalization rule fired, `events.log` records
`outcome=normalized … detail=normalized(<rules>)`.

Artifacts are Markdown with schema-versioned YAML front matter. Front matter
begins with `schema_version: 1`; a handoff that omits the key is treated as
version 1 (the CLI owns the current version), while an explicit different value
is rejected as a mismatch. Every handoff's front matter also carries the
`run_id` and `turn` of the turn it answers, matched exactly during validation,
and the turn templates name every key the validator requires. ForgeCycle
fills these turn facts when a handoff omits them. Runtime directories default
to mode `0700` and files to `0600`.

Each turn manifest also names `EVIDENCE_DIR`
(`<run-dir>/evidence/turn-NNN/`, created before the invocation). Agents write
logs, test reports and probes there instead of `/tmp`. The directory is outside
the worktree, so writing to it is never a repository mutation. When
`worktree.copy_ignored` provisioned files, the manifest lists them as
`PROVISIONED_FILES`; agents must not create, modify or delete them. A task
run started by a roadmap run whose decisions exist names its copy of them as
`ROADMAP_DECISIONS`: binding human answers that no role may ask
again and that never widen the task's scope.

```text
001-planner-plan.md
002-builder-result.md
003-reviewer-review.md
004-human-feedback.md
005-reviewer-review.md
```

Invalid and incomplete responses never consume a valid turn number.

## Upstream decomposition contract

`forgecycle roadmap decompose` is a separate assessment turn before a run. Its Decomposer
candidate returns schema-versioned JSON described by
`schemas/decomposition.schema.json`. ForgeCycle validates the assessment, required
task fields, unique stable IDs, and dependencies on earlier tasks before writing a
roadmap, source-plan snapshot, and self-contained Markdown task files to a new
repository directory. It also writes `roadmap.json`, the machine-readable
manifest described by `schemas/roadmap.schema.json`:

```json
{
  "schema_version": 1,
  "source_plan": "source-plan.md",
  "decisions": "decisions.md",
  "tasks": [
    { "id": "FC01", "title": "Add the store", "file": "FC01.md", "depends_on": [] },
    { "id": "FC02", "title": "Expose the API", "file": "FC02.md", "depends_on": ["FC01"] }
  ]
}
```

Array order is execution order. IDs match `^FC[0-9]{2,}$` and are unique, and
each task depends only on earlier tasks; the same graph check validates the
decomposition and the manifest. `file` and the optional `source_plan` and
`decisions` are relative to the manifest's directory, and `file` and
`decisions` end in `.md`.
Hand-written manifests use the same format. Tooling reads task order and
prerequisites from `roadmap.json`, never from the Markdown roadmap. Before proposing boundaries, the candidate investigates
relevant implementation, tests, structure, and integration points. Each task's
context records the observed repository evidence, architectural constraints, and
component-level change guidance that justify its scope and dependencies. This is
provisional guidance rather than an authoritative file-level implementation plan:
the task Planner re-investigates its selected base revision and chooses exact
changes and tests. Decomposition has no run state or completion authority. Each
task starts an ordinary Planner–Builder–Reviewer run when selected by the user.

## Plan contract

The plan records repository findings, controlling guidelines, assumptions,
in/out scope, stable acceptance IDs (`AC01`), concrete file-level implementation
instructions, and structured required tests with stable IDs (`T01`) and exact
commands. It also records risks, Builder instructions, and an objective done
checklist. Its status is `planned` or `needs_human`. Required-test commands
must pass the configured command lint rules (`lint.command_rules` with
`applies_to: plan`). A violation is a repairable field error that quotes the
rule's message. A required test that reads a gate's output carries
`after_gate: true` (see [Gates](/documentation/reference/protocol/#gates)).

## Builder contract

Builder reports `completed`, `partial`, or `blocked`, along with exact base/head
revisions, changed files, acceptance evidence, and structured test commands,
outcomes, and evidence matched to every planned test ID,
deviations, remaining work, blockers, and review notes. The reported test IDs
must be exactly the currently required set, each with an equivalent command. `completed` requires every test to have passed, except gated and
after-gate tests, which may be `not_run`; a turn with other failing or
`not_run` tests reports `partial` and explains what remains. A turn ends with
the agent's final message: nothing resumes it, so a Builder that starts work
in the background and waits for it never commits. A
changing turn creates exactly one descendant commit and leaves a clean
worktree. The one-commit rule
is per turn: each later turn adds one new commit on top of the previous turns'
commits, and amending, rebasing, or squashing an earlier turn's commit is a
protocol violation. A blocked or declared
no-change turn creates no commit and also leaves the worktree clean.

Sometimes a Builder commits cleanly exactly once but its handoff fails
validation and repair. ForgeCycle then records the commit as `unaccepted_head`, and the resumed Builder manifest carries `UNACCEPTED_HEAD`. That
recovery turn may re-emit the handoff with no new commit, or add exactly one
follow-up commit. The range is measured from where the unaccepted commit's
turn started, and the commit counts toward the turn whose handoff is
accepted.

## Review contract

Reviewer returns `done`, `changes_requested`, `blocked`, or `needs_human`. It
assesses both latest and cumulative diffs — recording the reviewed
`base_revision` and `head_revision` in front matter — and includes a non-empty
`criteria`
array covering every acceptance ID with status `satisfied`, `unsatisfied`, or
`blocked`. It reruns every required check that is not gated and records a
non-empty `tests` array with independently produced outcome evidence for every
currently required test ID — every test entry carries evidence, including `not_run` entries, which state
the reason the test was not run. A `findings` key is always present (an explicit
empty array when there are none), assigning stable finding IDs (`F001`) with
severity, location, status, and evidence. Three successive reviews with the same open finding set and no newly
resolved or superseded finding pause as a no-progress cycle.
Reviewer may add a stable test when review reveals new evidence. The review must
record a justification, a failing addition produces a Builder follow-up, and the
test remains part of the required set for every later turn. An added test's
command must reference repository files or files under `EVIDENCE_DIR`. The
built-in `no-tmp-scripts` rule rejects `/tmp` paths in added tests, and
`lint.command_rules` with `applies_to: review_added` add project rules.

Every review manifest names `LAST_REVIEWED_HEAD` and
`CHANGED_SINCE_LAST_REVIEW`, the delta since the previous review. When the
project configures `review.evidence_reuse_paths` and every changed path
matches, the manifest says `EVIDENCE_REUSE: allowed`. The review may then mark
a required test `reused: true`, carrying over the previous review's passed
result. Reuse anywhere else is a repairable validation error.

### Gates

A project may configure `review.gates`, operator-written commands for long
suites. Planning, building, and review manifests list them as
`GATES:` lines (`- <gate-id>: <command>`). A required test whose command is
equivalent to a gate's command is gated:

- The Builder manifest names gated tests under `GATED_TESTS:`. A Builder may
  report them `not_run` with evidence and still return `completed`.
- A required test that reads a gate's output, or must otherwise run after a
  gated test, carries `after_gate: true`. The gates run after the
  Builder's turn, so the Builder manifest lists these tests under
  `AFTER_GATE_TESTS:`, and a Builder reports them `not_run` and may still
  return `completed`. Reviewer runs them like any test that is not gated: the
  gates have already run when the review starts, and the review manifest
  lists them too. A plan may set `after_gate` only on a test that is not
  gated, and only when another required test is gated. The flag is part of
  the test's definition: ForgeCycle fills it in a review that omits it, a
  review may not change it, and a test the review adds may set it under the
  same rules. A Builder's own `after_gate` value is ignored.
- Before each review, ForgeCycle runs every gate a required test uses, once per
  gate, in the worktree at the reviewed HEAD. The gate runs with `/bin/sh -c`,
  in its own process group, with `FORGECYCLE_GATE` and `FORGECYCLE_GATE_HEAD`
  set, and writes its output to `RUN_DIR/gates/<head>/<gate-id>.log`. A
  finished run is stored beside its log as `<gate-id>.json`. A later review of
  the same HEAD and command reuses that result instead of running the gate
  again, so a review retried after a crash does not repeat a long suite.
- The review manifest lists `GATE_RESULTS:` with one line per gated test:
  status, exit code or timeout, duration, log, and whether the result was
  reused. The review must report each gated test with exactly that status and
  without `reused`. A mismatch is a repairable validation error.
- A gate that exits non-zero or reaches `timeout_seconds` is a `failed`
  result, which the review reports like any failing test. A timed-out result
  is not stored, so the next review runs the gate again. On a timeout or an
  interruption (Ctrl-C or SIGTERM) ForgeCycle stops the whole
  process group, escalating from SIGTERM to SIGKILL after 10 seconds, and
  then runs the gate's `cleanup`.
- A gate must leave HEAD and the tracked and untracked files as it found
  them; ignored build output is allowed. A gate that changes them, cannot
  start, or is interrupted stops the run with `stop_kind: gate_failure`
  before Reviewer is invoked.
An unresolved finding must remain present in later reviews until it is explicitly
marked resolved or superseded; silently dropping it is a protocol failure.

## States

```text
planning → awaiting_plan_approval → building → reviewing
    ▲                                  │          │
    │                                  │          ├─ changes_requested → building
    │                                  │          ├─ blocked
    │                                  │          ├─ paused / needs_human
    │                                  │          └─ awaiting_final_approval → done
    └──────── human rejection ─────────┴───────────────────────────────────────
```

Stable stored states are `planning`, `awaiting_plan_approval`, `building`,
`reviewing`, `awaiting_final_approval`, `paused`, `blocked`, `done`, `failed`, and
`abandoned`. `blocked` is recoverable with changed conditions or human feedback;
`failed` means an orchestration invariant or configuration needs repair.

While a run is stopped, `state.json` records `reason` (free text),
`resume_state` (the phase `task resume` re-enters), and `stop_kind`, a
stable classification of the stop: `approval_gate`,
`needs_human`, `technical_block`, `no_progress`, `agent_failure`,
`unaccepted_head`, `read_only_mutation`, `builder_invariant`,
`review_invariant`, `gate_failure`, or `pause_requested`. An optional `stop_detail` refines it:
the checkpoint of an approval gate, the failure category of an agent failure
(for example `quota_exhausted` or `mixed`), or the cause of a gate failure
(`interrupted`, `start_failed`, `worktree_mutated`). All four are cleared when the run leaves the
stopped state. Tooling should key recovery off `stop_kind`, not `reason`;
[recovery](/documentation/guides/recovery/#reading-a-stop) lists the next action for each.

A signal leaves a task run in one of two places. A gate it cuts
short records `gate_failure (interrupted)`. An agent turn it cuts short
records nothing: the agent CLI is stopped (SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after 10
seconds), no further candidate is tried, and the task run stays in its
active state, reported as `interrupted` like a task run whose process was
killed. Git checks of the worktree are never cut short, so an interrupt is
never mistaken for a mutation. A signal is never resumed past.

`forgecycle pause` asks the running task run or roadmap run to
stop once its current turn ends, gates included. It writes the file
`pause-request` into the run's directory, and the process advancing the run
checks it before it starts the next turn. A task command started by a
roadmap run's driver also honors its roadmap run's request, so `pause`
writes only that one for a roadmap run. The task run then records `paused`
with `stop_kind: pause_requested` and `resume_state` set to the turn it was
about to start, removes its request, and exits 21. Taking or releasing a
run's process lock removes a request, so one a process never honored does
not pause a later command. `forgecycle unpause` removes a pending request, or
continues the paused run with `task resume` or `roadmap resume`. A pause is
never resumed past by `--auto-resume`.

With `--auto-resume` on `task run` or `task resume`, a task run
resumes itself after a stop whose recovery is a plain resume with no input,
at most once between two accepted handoffs. `state.json` then records
`auto_resume_turn`, the turn at the last automatic resume, and
`auto_resumes`, the number of automatic resumes over the task run's life.
Both are optional and survive leaving the stopped state. A handoff that ends
in a `review_invariant` or `builder_invariant` stop counts in `turn` but is
not accepted. When the stop that remains follows an automatic resume with no
accepted handoff since, its stop block adds `forgecycle: stop:
auto_resume=used turn=<n>`.

A task run started by a roadmap run records it in `state.json` as
`roadmap_run_id` and `roadmap_task_id` (for example `FC02`). The roadmap run
passes them to its child `task run` as the environment variables
`FORGECYCLE_ROADMAP_RUN_ID` and `FORGECYCLE_ROADMAP_TASK_ID`. ForgeCycle
validates them (an invalid value exits 65) and unsets both before it starts
anything, so adapter CLIs and gates never inherit them: an agent running
`forgecycle task run` inside a worktree does not tag its task run with the
roadmap run.

State is stored in atomically replaced `.forgecycle/task-runs/<task-run-id>/state.json`. A repository-wide directory
lock permits one active or paused run, while a per-run process lock prevents two
commands from advancing the same state concurrently.

## Roadmap runs

A roadmap run (`forgecycle roadmap run`) executes a `roadmap.json`
with no operator between tasks. Each task runs as an ordinary task run, with
its own state, handoffs, branch, worktree, and approval policy, started as a
child `forgecycle task run <task.md> --base <integration-head>` at the
repository root with inherited output. The child records
`roadmap_run_id` and `roadmap_task_id` (see above).

**Decisions.** The decomposition's questions (schema version 3:
`question`, `context`, `impact`, `options` with `choice` and `consequences`,
`recommended` with `choice` and `reason`, and `affects`) are written for a human
who has not just read the code, by the shared rules in
`prompts/writing_questions.md`; a question missing a part, with one option, or
with a multi-line question or choice is rejected and repaired. They are
numbered Q01, Q02, … and written to `decisions.md`, one `## <ID>: <title>`
section each with **Context**, **What depends on it**, **Affects**, **Options**,
and **Recommended** paragraphs, then an `Unclear:` and an `Answer:` line. Each
marker line, and what follows it up to the next marker line or level-two
heading, holds the human's text; agent text that would read as a heading or
marker gets one leading space. The `**Recommended: X.**` (or a hand-written
`Recommended: X`) line is the answer `--accept-defaults` takes. Humans may add
sections. `roadmap questions` asks the `decomposer` candidates, read-only
(`schemas/roadmap-questions.schema.json`, version 2), to rewrite every decision
listed as `UNCLEAR_DECISIONS` under its own ID so it answers the human's
`Unclear:` text, which the rewrite quotes as **You asked**, and for decisions
still missing, which it appends. `roadmap run` refuses to start while a
decision is unanswered or unclear (exit 65); on a terminal it asks each
unanswered one, where `?` marks it unclear, and saves the answers. It snapshots the
answered document to the roadmap run's `decisions.md`; each task run copies
that file when it starts, records it as `roadmap_decisions`, and names it in
every turn manifest as `ROADMAP_DECISIONS`. `task resume --feedback` on a
`needs_human` stop of a roadmap run's task run appends the feedback to the
roadmap run's `decisions.md` as an `H` decision, quoting the stopping handoff's
Assumptions and Questions (plan) or Follow-up Instructions (review), so later
task runs receive it. Planner and Reviewer prompts carry the same
question-writing rules, so a `needs_human` handoff states each question as a
`### Q1:` subsection with the same parts.

**Integration rule.** Tasks run strictly in manifest order. Task N's base is
the integration head after task N−1. The roadmap run creates
`forgecycle/roadmap/<roadmap-run-id>` at its base (an `update-ref` with an
all-zero old value, so an existing branch is never reused) and moves it only
by compare-and-swap `git update-ref`, to each done task run's recorded
`head_revision`, never its branch tip. Only the roadmap run moves the
integration branch, so integration is always a fast-forward: no merge commits,
no conflicts, and every state of the integration branch is exactly a head
Reviewer reviewed as `done` on the base it was built on. Before moving the ref
it checks that the task run started on the integration head it was given,
that its head descends from it, and that the branch is not checked out in any
worktree. User branches and task run branches are never touched. Every step
can be repeated, so `roadmap resume` recovers from a crash at any point,
including adopting a task run the roadmap run started but did not record.

**State.** `.forgecycle/roadmap-runs/<roadmap-run-id>/` (mode 0700) holds a
snapshot of the manifest (`roadmap.json`; task files are read when their task
run starts, so a pending task can be refined while the roadmap run is
stopped), the resolved `decisions.md` when the manifest names one or a
`needs_human` answer was carried forward, `state.json` (atomically replaced, mode 0600,
`schemas/roadmap-run-state.schema.json`), `result.md` when it finishes, and a
`.process.lock/` owner PID. Stored states are `running`, `stopped`, `done`,
`failed`, and `abandoned`; a `running` roadmap run with no live process lock
is reported as interrupted, which is computed and never stored. Task statuses
are `pending`, `running`, `done`, and `skipped`, and each task lists every
task run (attempt) it had.

**Stops.** A roadmap run never resolves a recorded stop itself, except that
`roadmap resume` resumes a task run that paused on request. It stops at
the first stop that remains (after `--auto-resume`, when given) and records
`reason`, `stop_kind`, and `stop_detail`, cleared when it continues:

- `task_run_stopped`: the detail is the task run's stop kind; the exit code
  mirrors the task run (20, 21, or 22).
- `task_run_start_failed`: a child created no task run; the detail and the
  exit code are the child's (for example 65, or 21 when another task run
  holds the reservation).
- `integration_blocked`: `checked_out` leaves the roadmap run `stopped`
  (exit 21); `moved` or `not_descendant` marks it `failed` (exit 22).
- `pause_requested`: `forgecycle pause` asked for a pause; the current task
  run paused with it, or the roadmap run stopped before starting or resuming
  a task run (exit 21). The roadmap run removes its request.

`roadmap resume` decides from the current task's latest task run's
`state.json`: `done` is integrated and the next task starts, `abandoned` is
retried with a new task run on the unchanged integration head, an
interrupted one or one that paused on request is continued with
`task resume`, a live one is refused with exit 21, and any other stopped one
is reported with nothing else done. The
[recovery guide](/documentation/guides/recovery/#roadmap-run-stops) lists the next action for
each stop.

## Definition of done

`done` requires all acceptance criteria satisfied, all findings resolved or
superseded, independent test evidence, a clean worktree, valid Builder commit
history, and scope/guideline compliance. Planner and Reviewer may clarify criteria but cannot
weaken or expand them without immutable human approval.

## Configuration at turn boundaries

Before each task turn, ForgeCycle loads the current merged configuration. The selected policy name remains in task state, while its candidate lists and other settings come from the current files. A turn uses one loaded configuration. Invalid configuration stops advancement before the next turn (exit 65). Task state no longer contains an effective-config snapshot path.
